sources.citation: Burns DJ, Stevenson P, Murphy PJC. PFAS removal from groundwaters using Surface-Active Foam Fractionation. Remediation. 2021;1–15.

evidence_chunks.text: Results from a field trial commissioned for the Australian Department of Defence at the Army Aviation Centre Oakey evaluated the effectiveness of the Surface‐Active Foam Fractionation (SAFF) process at removing per‐ and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in groundwater. The study showed that the SAFF process is effective in removing ≥99.5% of the aggregate of perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), perfluorohexane sulfonate (PFHxS), and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) in PFAS‐contaminated groundwater, and consistently achieved the criteria for these PFAS species prescribed in the Australian PFAS National Environmental Management Plan (HEPA, 2020) water quality specification, and exceeded such by a factor of 3.3 over the 12 month study period.

The water treatment plant installed to treat PFAS at the AACO site comprises a lead Surface‐Active Foam Fractionation (SAFF) process followed by an anionic exchange resin (AIX) polishing process with groundwater extracted from a third‐party installed extraction well network presenting an average aggregate concentration of PFOS and PFHxS of 3.81 μg/L… The average concentration of PFOA in the feedwater is 0.48 μg/L.

The field trial demonstrated that the removal (i.e., separation and concentration) extent of PFAS species due to SAFF is closely correlated with the adsorption coefficient of the molecules at the gas–liquid interface. When the reported adsorption coefficient is greater than approximately 1.0 × 10−6 m, practically all of the PFAS species, including PFOS, PFHxS, and PFOA, were removed by SAFF. Longer‐chain PFAS species that benefit from higher adsorption coefficients are easier to remove than shorter‐chain species that exhibit lower adsorption coefficient values.

It is noted that the presence of dissolved electrolytes arising from the site groundwater being classified as hard is believed to enhance the adsorption coefficients, and so SAFF is likely to become still more effective in brackish, saline, and reverse osmosis reject waters.

evidence_chunks.section: P1 Section 2.1 The foam fractionation process
evidence_chunks.text: In the simplest invocation of foam fractionation, gas (typically air) is bubbled through an aqueous solution of amphiphiles so that they adsorb to the surface of rising bubbles, which form a froth/foam layer above the liquid pool, and this can be removed/collapsed to form a “foamate” liquid that is enriched in the amphiphile. The residual liquid at the bottom of the column is depleted in the amphiphile.

evidence_chunks.section: P1 Section 2.1 The foam fractionation process
evidence_chunks.text: The practical implementation of foam fractionation at a commercial scale… involves consideration of, for instance, design geometry, method of bubble production, gas flow rate, foamate management, and opportunities for process intensification… the gas flow rate and bubble size dictate the hydrodynamic condition of the foam.

source_limitations: Field trial reports aggregate PFAS removal and adsorption-coefficient trends but provides limited raw time-resolved data on gas flow rates, bubble size distributions, and foamate volume reduction factors.
Focuses on long‑chain PFAS (PFOS, PFHxS, PFOA); behavior of very short‑chain PFAS is not characterized in detail.

sources.citation: Smith SJ, Wiberg K, McCleaf P, Ahrens L. Pilot-Scale Continuous Foam Fractionation for the Removal of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) from Landfill Leachate. ACS ES&T Water. 2022;2:841–851.

evidence_chunks.text: Pilot-Scale Continuous Foam Fractionation for the Removal of Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substances (PFAS) from Landfill Leachate.

This article investigates a pilot-scale continuous foam fractionation process for PFAS removal from landfill leachate, systematically varying operating parameters such as air flow rate, contact time, and foam fraction, and evaluating removal efficiencies for multiple PFAS classes.

The mass balance for the continuous tests ranged from about two-thirds to near complete closure (approximately 66% to 104%, depending on experiment), while for the batch experiment the mass balance closed only to about half when considering either the bottom or top effluent samples, indicating PFAS accumulation within the foam column and potential aerosol losses.

The pilot system treated real landfill leachate on-site to avoid changes in PFAS speciation during transport, demonstrating that foam fractionation can remove a wide range of perfluoroalkyl carboxylic acids and sulfonates from complex, saline matrices.

source_limitations: Only limited text was visible directly from the inspected PDF and associated open-access copy; detailed numerical values for gas flow, residence time, and enrichment factors are not fully captured here.
Study focuses on landfill leachate; extrapolation to other matrices (e.g., groundwater, municipal wastewater) must consider different organic matter and co‑surfactant profiles.

sources.citation: Smith SJ, Lewis JF, Wiberg K, Ahrens L. Foam fractionation for removal of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances: Towards closing the mass balance. Science of the Total Environment. 2023;871:162080.

evidence_chunks.text: Foam fractionation for removal of per‑ and polyfluoroalkyl substances: Towards closing the mass balance.

The study extends pilot-scale foam fractionation of PFAS-contaminated industrial water by explicitly quantifying PFAS distribution between influent, foamate, effluent, and intermediate water layers to evaluate mass balance closure and potential PFAS losses from the system.

Mass balance analysis showed that, although high removal efficiencies from the water phase were achieved for many long-chain PFAS, a fraction of PFAS accumulated in the upper water layer of the column rather than in the collected foam, and some losses could not be accounted for, emphasizing the need to consider all phases when assessing foam fractionation performance.

The work highlights that common performance indicators such as percentage removal of dissolved PFAS and enrichment in the foam can be misleading if mass balance closure is poor, and recommends including detailed volume reduction factors and PFAS inventories in all phases for process evaluation.

source_limitations: Only the first-page abstract and selected portions of the PDF were accessible for detailed inspection; specific numeric removal and enrichment values are not fully reproduced here.
The study focuses on an industrial water matrix (including landfill leachate-related systems); performance in low-organic groundwater or municipal wastewater may differ.

Table S1: Physical parameters for foam fractionation experiments. System Parameters Consistent Across All Experiments – Column Height 60 cm; Column Inner Diameter 5 cm; Solution Fill Height 55 cm; Air flow rate 0.47 L/min; Air pressure 19.4 kPa; Vacuum Pressure 18.6 kPa; Diffusion Stone Pore size 0.5 micron.

evidence_chunks.section: Main article (described in publisher abstract) / SI context
evidence_chunks.text: Two representative long-chain PFAS, perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid potassium salt (K-PFOS) as well as two representative short-chain PFAS, perfluorobutanoic acid (PFBA) and perfluorobutanesulfonic acid potassium salt (K-PFBS) were used in experiments with synthetic groundwater.

Table S2 reports initial PFAS concentrations in synthetic groundwater, with experimental sets including mixtures where PFBA, PFBS, PFOA, and PFOS are each present at tens of thousands of ng/L (e.g., ~40,000–50,000 ng/L) and other sets with lower concentrations down to a few hundred ng/L, enabling evaluation of concentration effects on removal and enrichment.

Table S3: Initial PFAS concentrations in groundwater from former Loring Air Force Base (AFB) and a military installation (MI) located in the eastern United States, listing PFBA, PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA, PFOA, PFNA, PFBS, PFHxS, PFHpS, PFOS, and 6:2 FTS, with PFOS and PFHxS in the low µg/L range and short-chain PFAAs in the hundreds of ng/L.

Table S4 summarizes groundwater properties for AFB and MI, including pH (8.17 and 5.65), conductivity (0.168 and 0.109 mS/cm), and salinity (0.02 and 0.05 ppt), indicating differing ionic strengths and acidity for evaluation of water-chemistry impacts on foam fractionation.

Section SI and subsequent figures describe experiments with cationic co‑surfactants (e.g., CTAB, DTAB, Polyquaternium-10) injected at controlled mass flow rates into the foam fractionation column, with measurements of Sauter mean bubble diameter over time and foamate volume, demonstrating how co‑surfactant choice affects bubble size, foam stability, volume reduction factor (VRF), and PFAS enrichment.

source_limitations: The main article HTML/PDF could not be directly accessed due to access restrictions; experimental conditions and PFAS compositions are taken from the open supplementary PDF and publisher summaries.
While the study includes both synthetic and natural groundwater, detailed time‑series removal curves for individual PFAS are referenced but not fully reproduced here.

sources.citation: Lee YC, Wang PY, Lo SL, Huang CP. Recovery of perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoate (PFOA) from dilute water solution by foam flotation. Sep Purif Technol. 2017;173:280–285.

evidence_chunks.text: The separation and recovery of surfactants, namely, Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) and Perfluorooctanoate (PFOA) was conducted using foam flotation process aided by metallic activators, including Al(III), Fe(III), La(III), Ca(II), Fe(II), and K(I). The PFOS removal efficiency followed the following decreasing order: Fe(III) La(III) > Al(III) > Ca(II) > Fe(II) > K(I). Both PFOS and FPOA had a removal efficiency of > 99% in the presence of 11.5 mM of Fe(III) in 5 min.

High Fe(III) dose and elevated initial PFOS and PFOA concentration enhanced surfactant removal. PFOS and PFOA removal also increased with decreasing pH with maximum removal occurring at the lowest pH of 2.3 studied; whereas no significant removal was observed at pH ≥ 6. At high pH, hydroxide ion (OH−) competed with PFOS or PFOA for Fe3+ and formed ferric hydroxo species that impeded surfactant removal.

By adjusting the pH of the concentrate scum to 7.0, approximately 84–91% of PFOS and PFOA could be recovered. Foam flotation using ferric ion as activator, is a simple, fast, and cost-effective method… for the separation and recovery of PFOS and PFOA from dilute water solutions.

source_limitations: Only the abstract and bibliographic information were accessible via the EPA HERO record; detailed column geometry, gas flow, and bubble-size data are not available from the inspected page.
Study focuses on PFOS and PFOA in relatively simple dilute solutions with added metallic activators; behavior in complex natural waters or with short‑chain PFAS is not addressed.

sources.citation: SERDP/ESTCP Project: Low-Cost, Passive In Situ Treatment of PFAS-Impacted Groundwater Using Foam Fractionation in an Air Sparge Trench. SERDP-ESTCP project description page.

evidence_chunks.text: The overarching goal of this project is to demonstrate and validate the use of a novel remedial technology capable of passively treating per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS)-impacted groundwater in situ. This project's approach utilizes conventional sparge trench technology coupled with the recent development of foam fractionation technology and foam recovery/reconstitution to remove PFAS from groundwater.

The approach for this project employs the use of a conventional air sparge trench to intercept a shallow PFAS-impacted groundwater plume… For PFAS, the sparging bubbles provide a high air-water interfacial area that facilitates “stripping” of the surface-active PFAS from the groundwater. This sparging process results in formation of a foam on the water surface, which can be subsequently removed via a vacuum and/or skimming system, resulting in orders of magnitude decreases in bulk groundwater PFAS concentrations.

PFAS concentration factors are typically in the range of 1-L of reconstituted foam to 5000-L of groundwater. This low volume, high concentration recovered PFAS can then be treated via conventional high temperature incineration or treated via promising technologies such as electrochemical oxidation (ECO) and enhanced contact plasma (ECP).

source_limitations: Project page summarizes objectives and conceptual design but does not yet report detailed quantitative removal data, PFAS speciation, or full mass-balance closure for the in situ system.

Reactor geometry (trench dimensions), gas flow rates, and long‑term operational performance metrics are not specified on the inspected page; additional reports would be needed for full quantitative assessment.
